excerpt: Paano magtanim ng melon? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant milon (melon), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant milon. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

How Filipino farmers grow melon, both the netted kind and honeydew, in the dry months: seed sprouted and planted in hills or set out from trays, vines run on the ground over mulch, and fruits cut when they smell sweet and come away from the stalk. It is a short guide for small lowland farms, since fewer farmers grow melon than pakwan.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for cucurbits](/land-preparation/cucurbit-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [milon varieties sold here](/crop-varieties/melon). If the leaves turn pale later on, the [milon nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/melon-nutrient-deficiency) helps you find what is missing. For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng gulay](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-gulay), [vegetables in the Philippines](/crops/vegetables-philippines).
When to plant milon

Melon needs hot, dry weather while the fruits ripen, because rain at that time splits the fruits and makes them less sweet. Lowland farmers plant at the start of the dry season so the harvest falls in the driest months, on loose, well drained soil.
What you plant
Seed. Melon seed is costly, so most farmers sprout it first in a damp cloth and either plant it straight in the hills or raise it in trays and set out the seedlings once they have a few true leaves.
Paano magtanim ng melon, step by step
Early kinds can be picked from about 65 days after planting, as growers in Tarlac report. Larger kinds and honeydew take longer. The crop is ready about 65 days after sowing.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 21 days before sowing: Plow and harrow the field
items.text: Plow and harrow two or three times until the soil is loose and airy. Pick a field that drains well and has not grown melon, pakwan or other gourds lately.

items.title: 5 days before sowing: Manure the rows and lay mulch
items.text: Work well rotted manure or compost into the rows with a basal dose of complete fertilizer such as 14 14 14. Many growers cover raised beds with plastic mulch and punch planting holes along the middle.

items.title: 2 days before sowing: Sprout the seed
items.text: Soak the seed for a few hours, wrap it in a damp cloth and keep it warm and shaded until the tiny roots show.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Sowing day: Plant the sprouted seed
items.text: Plant one or two sprouted seeds a hill, root down, and cover lightly with fine soil. Water gently.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 5: Guard the seedlings
items.text: Check the young plants every day or two for leaf beetles and cutworms, which can wipe out a stand in the first weeks. Replant empty hills.

items.title: Day 7: Water lightly and evenly
items.text: Water the hills or run water in the furrows when the topsoil dries, a little at a time. Never let water stand around the stems.

items.title: Day 14: Thin to one plant
items.text: Keep the strongest plant in each hill and pull the rest.

items.title: Day 21: Side dress as the vines run
items.text: When the vines begin to run, side dress with urea a hand span from the stem and cover it. Weed the rows by hand before the vines cover the ground.

items.title: Day 30: Help the fruits set
items.text: If few bees come, touch an open male flower to the female flowers, the ones with a small ball behind the petals, early in the morning. Do not spray while the flowers are open.

items.title: Day 35: Keep the best fruits
items.text: Keep a few well shaped fruits on each vine and remove the crooked or stung ones. Rest each fruit on straw or the plastic mulch so it does not touch wet soil.

items.title: Day 40: Potash for sweetness
items.text: Once the fruits are the size of an egg, side dress with muriate of potash or complete fertilizer and water it in.

items.title: Day 55: Cut back the water
items.text: As the fruits near ripeness, water less so they do not crack and their flesh turns sweeter.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Day 65: Pick ripe fruits
items.text: A ripe netted melon smells sweet, its skin turns from green to tan under the net, and it slips off the stalk with a light push. Honeydew does not slip: cut it when the skin turns creamy and slightly waxy.

items.title: Day 66: Handle gently
items.text: Carry the fruits in lined baskets or crates, keep them in the shade, and sell them within a few days.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for milon
Spacing
Rows wide enough for the vines to run, often 1.5 to 2 meters apart, with one plant every half meter or so along the row. Big fruited kinds get more room.
Water
Light, even watering by hand or furrow, more while the fruits swell and less as they ripen. Water must never stand around the stems.
Fertilizer

Well rotted manure or compost and a basal dose of complete fertilizer such as 14 14 14 before planting, urea when the vines start to run, and muriate of potash or complete fertilizer once the fruits form. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-vegetables-philippines).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Thinning to one plant a hill, weeding by hand before the vines spread, plastic mulch or straw under the fruits, hand pollination when bees are few, and removal of crooked or stung fruits. Farmers check often for beetles and fruit flies.
When and how to harvest

Netted melons are ripe when they smell sweet, turn tan under the net and slip from the stalk with a light push. Honeydew is cut when its skin turns creamy and waxy. Fruits are handled gently, kept in the shade and sold within a few days.
Common mistakes when planting milon

items: Timing the crop so it ripens in the rainy months, which splits the fruits and spoils the sweetness.
Picking before the fruit slips or smells sweet, so it never sweetens off the vine.
Planting where melon, pakwan or other gourds just grew, so soil diseases carry over.
Watering heavily near harvest, which cracks the fruits and dilutes the flavor.
Leaving too many fruits on one vine, which gives small, bland melons.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of milon
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Have the soil tested and feed by the result, with enough potash for sweet fruits.
Buy good hybrid seed suited to the lowlands and sprout it before planting so none is wasted.
Use plastic mulch on raised beds with drip irrigation for clean fruits and steady water.
Scout weekly and use integrated pest management for thrips, aphids, beetles and fruit fly.
Rotate with rice, corn or beans and keep two seasons between gourd crops on the same field.
